Presidential Ramblings
By Steve Hansen
Greetings,
A plea to our newer members, please read the article titled: “Here Is What You Missed” inside this
newsletter, along with all of the other great content.
We conducted an informal canvass of other turning
clubs in North America and can report that similar
sized clubs that produce similar programming and
content are generally more expensive than our
Guild. In light of our growing losses for hosting
Guest Turners, The Board of Directors is increasing
the All Day Demo rate from $35 to $40 and the Visiting Demonstrator Class tuition from $165 to $200.
To underline the value that we think we produce, it
is not uncommon for other clubs to charge $50 for
an all-day demo and $300 for a class day with the
same guest turners. Thank you for your understanding and continued support.
The President’s Challenge for January is Try Something New as shown to us by any of our recent demonstrators.
Steve
President’s Challenge:
•
November - “Natural Edge”
•
January - “Try Something New”
Here’s What You Missed!
By Steve Hansen
Here’s some of what you missed if you couldn’t
attend our last four knowledgeable presenters.
•
Why you need a CBN wheel in order to properly
sharpen M42 / CPM alloy steels.
•
How easy it is to make your own bent tools for
reaching tight spots inside a bowl.
•
A clever and simple way to turn off-centre.
•
Innovative method for jam chucking that you
probably have not seen before.
•
A wall thickness gauge that costs nothing and is
surprising versatile.
•
How to reduce sanding and remove tool marks
•
Profiling negative rake scrapers
•
What is a Bedan and how useful it is!
•
Sheer scraping with a gouge
For those of us that attended, both in person and
via Zoom we were entertained, inspired, and educated by some of the best instructors the turning
world has to offer. Now for the not so good news:
Our current loss rate is $2000 per guest speaker! The majority of our loss is derived from two
factors. One is under-whelming attendance at allday demonstrations. Reasons for not attending
might be: “I feel intimidated by these world class
turners.” – “I don’t turn spindles, so why should I
attend a spindle demonstration?” - “I am just
starting out, so I think it is a waste of time to watch
a master.” – and so on.
As it turns out, guest turners generally begin their
demos from a novice perspective and grow into the
presentation with more advanced topics/methods,
but all along you will find nuggets of information
which anyone, at any level can adopt. Suffice to
say, the novice turner is in the envious position of
learning more than anyone else.
Come to the demo! I truly believe you will be pleasantly surprised.
The other reason we lose money is by under charging for our all day demos and classes. We simply
take in much less than we spend in order to host
our guests! Obviously this is not a great trend to
stay on. Accordingly, those fees need to increase
and are now set at $40 & $200 respectively.
Remember, come to the demo!

In Memoriam – Dr. David Sweet, O.C.
David was born in Cranbrook, nestled in the heart
of the Rockies – a place that shaped his spirit and
love of nature. He embraced every opportunity
that life in that region offered: hiking, skiing,
hunting, photography and outdoor hockey.
From an early age, it was clear that David aspired
to excellence in everything he did. That drive led
him to become the president of his high school, a
ole that reflected his leadership and compassion
for others.
After graduating, David moved to Vancouver to
pursue his studies to be a dentist, setting the stage
for not only a successful private practice but an
extraordinary academic journey. After six years in
private practice he returned to UBC to teach.
Teaching was his passion and mentorship became
an important part of David’s life.
David went on to earn a Ph.D. in forensic medicine
from the University of Granada in Spain. His thesis
was the development of the recovery of DNA from
bitemarks, later nicknamed the “Sweet Swab”.
David’s research led to the start of the Bureau of
Legal Dentistry (BOLD) at UBC that specialized in
the application of forensic science methods to
dental evidence. Studying in Spain also led to special longtime friendships and the love of the Spanish culture.
David’s dedication and integrity earned him numerous awards and honours, culminating in this
appointment as an Officer of the Order of Canada
– a fitting recognition of a lifetime spent on advancing knowledge and serving others.
After an accomplished and fulfilling career, David
eventually retired but in true David fashion,
“retirement” didn’t mean slowing down. Instead,
he applied his skills to the art of woodturning and,
not surprisingly, David was superb at it. Every year
David was commissioned by the Canadian Botanical Association to make personalized awards for
the winners.
David’s life was a testament to curiosity, hard
work and excellence. From the mountains of Cranbrook to the lecture halls of Granada, from the
recognition of the Order of Canada to the hum of
his woodturning lathe, David lived each chapter of
his life with purpose and grace.
David had the rare ability to inspire those around
him – not only through his accomplishments, but
through his humility, kindness and generosity of
spirit.
Dr. David Sweet, OC
December 15, 1952 – September 17, 2025

Tech Talk
By Steve Hansen
This is an aggregate from September and October
meetings.
Brian Lunt shared his experience with a new spray
paint nozzle on some Rustoleum finishes that allow for adjustable spray patterns and flow rates,
which he found particularly useful for detailed and
curved surfaces.
Steve Hansen and Phil Winch shared their methods
for maintaining and cleaning spray nozzles, with
Phil using paint thinner in a jar for storage and Steve making sure to wipe the nozzle clean after use.
Sharpening using CBN wheels for high-speed steels
was mentioned, with Phil noting that a coarser
grind gave him better results. I think it is 80 grit
that he uses. The group also talked about different
profiles for negative rake scrapers, including Tom
Wirsing's technique which uses equal angles of 22
½ degrees on both sides which renders an included angle of 45 degrees. The side you touched up
last is the side you cut with-that’s the side that has
a tiny burr and allows the subtle removal of tool
marks.
Brian Lunt shared an incident involving cutting a
bowl blank. It involved a piece of wood that had a
bark inclusion and whilst cutting, the bark broke
away and rendered an unstable block which then
slammed against his hand…. 13 stitches later and
several weeks of recovery ensued. The warning is
to inspect everything that runs through the band
saw and think about “what could go wrong?”
The subject of carbide versus high speed steels was
brought up. The general consensus is that HSS
steels render a smoother cut but require occasional sharpening in your shop, sometimes frequent
depending on the timber being turned. Whereas
carbide tools generally are unable to produce as
clean of a cut as HSS, but do not require sharpening, instead relying on replacement bits.
Someone asked how Kevin Jesequel affixed cutting
tips-HSS steel- into his custom bent tools for hollowing. The answer is thick CA glue with activator
spray to cure. Be sure to align the bit in accordance
with the shank. To remove a bit, heat with a torch
and the glue will melt. To insert a new bit you may
need to ream out the old glue with a drill bit of the
same diameter. Repeat the affixing process as
above.
Online videos! Everyone watches them, but there
is an abundance of really poor turning videos which
collectively display poor method or unsafe practices. To help you weed out the bad, here are just a
few names to search for that are of quality technique: Allan or Stuart Batty, Nick Cook, Cindy Drozda, Richard Raffan, Ashley Harwood, Tomaslav Tomasic, Glenn Lucas. There are many others that are
good, but sadly there are way too many more that
are not. Try out these suggestions and are you are
on the right track.
Tech Talk is held on the Monday evening following
the Guild ZOOM session. The credentials for the
session are sent to all registered Guild members
and all are encouraged to participate in the freeflowing discussion centered on technical aspects of
woodturning.

Page 6
For those just starting out in woodturning, the
lathe is full of promise but also pitfalls. Short
meetings and casual chats spark ideas, but the real
learning happens at full-day demonstrations. If
you miss them, you miss the building blocks that
make turning safer, smoother, and more rewarding.
What Beginners Miss at Recent Full-Day Demos
•
Toolrest Height - Demonstrators showed how
toolrest height determines whether a cut is
clean or catches, and how to set it so the
cutting edge meets the wood at the right angle.
•
How to Hold a Gouge - They demonstrated
how grip, stance, and body movement matter
as much as the tool itself, showing how to anchor the gouge, roll it smoothly, and let the
bevel guide the cut.
•
Push, Pull, and Shear Cuts - Demonstrators explained the differences between push cuts, pull
cuts, shear cuts, and shear scraping, showing
each in action so beginners could see when and
why to use them.
•
Creating a Correct Tenon - They showed how a
tenon with crisp shoulders and proper diameter ensures safe, accurate workholding — and
why a poor tenon risks failure.
•
Using the Tailstock - Demonstrators highlighted how the tailstock adds stability, especially
when roughing or hollowing, and when to bring
it up for best support.
•
Gauging Wall Thickness - They shared tricks
with calipers, light reflection, and even sound
— plus demonstrated how a bent clothes‑handle tool can check thickness inside a hollow
form.
•
Texturing with a Wire Wheel - Demonstrators
showed how a wire wheel can add rustic texture or highlight grain patterns, while stressing
safe, controlled use.
•
What is a Bedan? - Demonstrators introduced
the bedan, showing its versatility for beads,
grooves, and parting cuts. They also demonstrated how it can be used like a skew, giving
beginners another tool for clean, precise cuts
and opening up new design possibilities.
•
Making a Hollowing Tool - Demonstrators
proved not every tool needs to be bought,
showing how to craft a simple hollowing tool
from steel rod or even repurposed Allen keys.
Online vs. In-Person Learning
Videos online can inspire, but they can’t replace
the depth of being there. At a demo you:
•
See the stance, grip, and body movement that
videos miss.
•
Hear the difference between clean cuts and
catches.
•
Ask questions and get immediate answers.
•
Watch the whole process, including mistakes
and corrections.
•
Connect with fellow turners and share the experience.
The Value of Showing Up
A full-day demo isn’t just a presentation — it’s a
classroom, a workshop, and a community all in
one. You see the entire journey: setup, roughing,
shaping, sanding, texturing, and finishing. That continuity teaches patience, problem-solving, and creativity — skills every beginner needs.
(Continued on page 7)
Why Full -Day Demos Matter for Beginning
Woodturners
By Don Gamble

November 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 7
How Beginners Can Truly Catch Up
If you’ve missed demos, the best way forward is
simple: attend the next one.
•
One day of focused learning can save months
of trial and error.
•
You’ll pick up safe habits that stick.
•
You’ll see techniques in real time, not just in
edited clips.
•
You’ll join a community that grows together.
Guild resources and mentors are helpful, but
they’re supplements — not substitutes. The fastest, most effective way to grow as a beginning
turner is to come out to the all-day demos.
Closing Thought
Woodturning isn’t just about shaping wood — it’s
about shaping skill, confidence, and creativity. Fullday demos are the guild’s most powerful classroom. Don’t miss them. Your future projects will
thank you.
(Continued from page 6)
Tech Tip - VariGrind Arm Spacer
By Brian Lunt
This is a guarantee that your VariGrind is always
put into the exact space each time so you do not
have to grind away good steel getting back to the
angle you were after.
Use basic ¾” x ¾” aluminum from local hardware
store cut into the correct lengths.
You can colour them to match the angle you want,
spindle gouge, bowl gouge etc
KMS Tools Group Rewards
Shopping at KMS Tools means you can help your
club earn credit - approximately 2% on your purchase. For instance, we recently used some of our
credit to buy the brand-new Laguna demo lathe
that we use for Focus on Fundamentals! All you
need to do is to link your name/phone number to
the GVWG and you’re done. The easiest way to do
this is to go online to: https://www.kmstools.com/
group-rewards and fill in a short form. In doing so,
you also become a KMS Club member and benefit
from better pricing on their full line of products. As
a friendly reminder if you are already a KMS Club
member, it is worthwhile to check that you are also
linked to the GVWG for us to receive the credits.

Safety Guidelines for Woodturning
You mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 20)

November 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 20
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
